intro: WELCOME. This is a realistic-opponent repertoire for the Queen's Gambit complex (1.d4 d5 2.c4), built the same way as the companion Sicilian Defense Encyclopedia: for every position, the main theoretical moves, common tries you'll actually meet, sharp/gambit lines, quiet positional systems, traps, and typical mistakes. PLANNED TABLE OF CONTENTS — Chapter 1: Understanding the Queen's Gambit (foundations — structures, breaks, plans). Chapter 2: The Queen's Gambit Declined, Main Lines (Orthodox). Chapter 3: The Exchange Variation and the Minority Attack. Chapter 4: The Tartakower, Lasker, and Cambridge Springs Defenses. Chapter 5: The Queen's Gambit Accepted. Chapter 6: The Slav Defense. Chapter 7: The Semi-Slav (Meran, Botvinnik, Moscow). Chapter 8: The Catalan. Chapter 9: The Chigorin, Albin Countergambit, and Other Rare Black Tries. Chapter 10: Traps and Tactics Compendium. Chapters will be built and appended one at a time, exactly as with the Sicilian book, with every line verified move-by-move for legality and spot-checked against current theory before being added.

THE CARLSBAD STRUCTURE (pawns on a2/b2/e3/f2/g2/h2 for White against a7/b7/c6/e6/f7/g7/h7 for Black, with an open d-file) is reached constantly from the Exchange Variation (Chapter 3) and defines an entire family of middlegames. White's standard long-term plan is THE MINORITY ATTACK: pushing b4-b5 to trade off queenside pawns and create a weakness on c6 (or an isolated/backward pawn) for Black to defend for the rest of the game, while Black looks for central or kingside counterplay, often involving ...Ne4 or a timely ...e5 break.

studies.title: Study 1.3c — The Isolated Queen's Pawn (IQP)

tree.commentAfter: THE ISOLATED QUEEN'S PAWN — White's d4-pawn has no friendly pawn on the c- or e-file to support it, making it a long-term structural target, but in exchange White gets extra central space, active piece play, and attacking chances, especially with pieces still on the board.

A completely typical IQP position — arguably the single most recurring pawn structure in all of 1.d4 chess (and much of 1.e4 chess too, via various move-transpositions). White's plan usually involves active piece play, sometimes even an eventual d5 pawn break; Black's plan is to blockade the d4/d5 squares (often with a knight on d5 or f5), trade pieces to reduce White's attacking chances, and target the pawn directly in any resulting endgame.
